title: DarkCore RAT: New Research Into Credential Theft and Stolen Browser Sessions
description: DarkCore is a newly discovered Remote Access Trojan (RAT) that facilitates credential theft, hidden desktop access, and session hijacking through a dedicated browser. It reuses stolen session cookies to access services like Gmail, WhatsApp, and MediaFire, routing traffic through victims' IP addresses to appear legitimate. The malware is distributed with a deceptive PDF-themed shortcut that downloads both a decoy document and a malicious executable. Operators can control infected machines via hidden virtual network computing (HVNC) and extend functionality through additional modules. The RAT communicates with a hardcoded command and control server and disguises itself using legitimate Windows process names. No official patch or remediation guidance is currently available.

aiSummary: DarkCore RAT is a Windows-based malware tool sold on cybercrime forums that enables attackers to steal credentials, hijack authenticated browser sessions, and control victim machines via hidden desktop access (HVNC). Its dedicated browser imports stolen session cookies and routes traffic through the victim's IP to evade detection. The malware is deployed using a PDF-themed shortcut that downloads a legitimate-looking report alongside a malicious executable, which is obfuscated to avoid user suspicion. The RAT communicates with a fixed C2 server over direct TCP and can load additional modules either in memory or as DLLs on disk. Persistence mechanisms appear disabled in the analyzed sample, but operators have control over session reuse and remote access features. Indicators of compromise and detailed analysis are provided by BlackFog researchers.
aiImpact: DarkCore enables attackers to steal user credentials and hijack authenticated sessions, potentially granting unauthorized access to email, messaging, and cloud storage accounts. The session hijacking feature allows attackers to appear as legitimate users by routing traffic through victims' IP addresses, complicating detection. Hidden desktop access allows full remote control of infected machines without user awareness. These capabilities can lead to data theft, privacy breaches, and further compromise of connected services.
